**a FourCC's wire form is the four characters, and the spelling is a bijection** (owner ruling, 2026-08-14; note **N109**). The type was `#[serde(transparent)]` over `[u8; 4]`, so `FormatUnsupported` — the refusal AGENTS' primary consumer is supposed to act on — reached an agent as `{"available": [[77,74,80,71],[89,85,89,86]]}` while the CLI table and the D13 message beside it said `MJPG, YUYV`. The ruling picks one spelling for all three. This row is the claim the spelling has to earn to be usable at all: the encoder (`Display`) and the decoder (`PixelFormat::parse`) are inverse over **every** four-byte value, not over the five this build names. The population is generated — the exhaustive cross product of every byte whose spelling can interact with another's (`\\`, `x`, both cases of every hex digit, and non-graphic bytes spanning the escape space) plus a seeded sweep of the whole space, 727 281 values — because note **N108**'s class applies here exactly: a list of the cases somebody thought of cannot constrain the byte nobody thought of. The injectivity half is separate and is the one a round trip alone would miss: a decoder that answered correctly for every string it was handed would still be useless if two formats spelled the same, since the ambiguity would be in what the wire carries. Alongside them the JSON claim itself, red against the transparent newtype in both directions — the array form is refused on the way in rather than accepted beside the string, because the owner chose one shape over "accept both" and a build that quietly took the array back would make that choice unobservable

**a sweep that announced itself ends the stream it opened**, on every path out of `engine::calibrate::run` (note **N88**, found by P5's review and belonging here because the law is the sweep executor's). D8 gives the terminal vocabulary two members — `SweepFinished` and `SweepInterrupted` — and `CalibrationProgress::is_terminal` is what every consumer branches on; before N88 three of `run`'s four exits after the `SweepStarted` emit returned with the stream still open, so a client that saw the start waited for ever. The three tests are one per hole and each drives a real refusal rather than a seam invented for it: a control slug that names no directory (the scripted double, because no device enumerates one and the fake must not learn to — E5), a **dangling symlink** where the pass's photo directory goes, and a **directory** in place of `session.json` so the closing commit fails at `rename` — root-proof, unlike a chmod, and the one arrangement the store's own fault menu cannot express, since a blanket `DiskFull` refuses the `begin_sweep` commit *before* the sweep announces itself. The property has no static signature — a `?` between the two events looks like any other `?` — so this is a counted selection and not a grep

the T5 method-count walk (docs/9 Part 2, note N28): every method the daemon's own into_rpc() registers is exercised over the fake and answers, on both transports — the exercised side recorded at the transport from the generated client's own spelling rather than listed beside it, so a wire method with no test stops the count — the one assertion that carries the row, proven red by deleting a call and pinned non-vacuous against the twenty-two crates/api pins rather than by a loop that could not fail; one non-vacuous assertion per answer, which the compiler requires for every method because an answer nobody reads is dead code; the registered set **partitioned** rather than filtered by hand now that four of its names belong to two subscriptions no ClientT can send — the unsubscribe half derived from api::SUBSCRIPTIONS and asserted to be a subset before it is subtracted, so removing a name nothing registered weakens nothing silently, and both counts pinned: twenty-two calls since P6c closed D10's list with the three `record_*` verbs, and twenty-two plus two per subscription registered (notes N29 and N57); and the recorder itself asserted to write down what crossed the wire and nothing else, refusals included

the two things the daemon says without being asked, over both transports (D10, docs/7 P4e-i): every subscription the daemon's own registration carries driven to a real delivery — a hotplug event off the daemon's own watch thread and a progress event out of a real sweep, decoded from frames that crossed a real WebSocket on the daemon's own AF_UNIX socket — with the population walked from api::SUBSCRIPTIONS so a subscription with no delivery test stops the walk rather than passing in silence, watched red by adding a third row to wire_surface! and seeing the walk name it; one upgraded connection carrying a subscription and a call at the same time, which is the duplex fact P4f's client transport has to be built against rather than discover, with the plain HTTP transport beside it unaffected; a subscriber that stops reading costing counted drops and never the daemon — the bound read from limits::WS_MESSAGE_BUFFER_CAPACITY rather than transcribed, the split between the two hops asserted exactly because both instants are signals rather than guesses (the reading subscriber taking the last event says the producer finished, the daemon's own loss count reaching the overflow says the stalled subscriber's task did), a second subscriber on the same source losing nothing, and the daemon still answering three refusals that discriminate while the slow one is stuck — watched red against a hand-applied send().await, which becomes a named nextest TIMEOUT rather than a hang; disconnect mid-sweep, both halves docs/7 names and rubric B6 spells — the sweep continues to a document engine::lifecycle reads back through the same function calibrate_status answers from, the subscription is reaped, and the server then stops, which is what a leaked bridging task would turn into a TIMEOUT; events emitted with nobody subscribed dropped and counted, both directions, so the same sweep with a subscriber attached adds nothing to the count; the per-connection subscription bound refused as a -32006 answer to the subscribe call before any handler runs, with a second connection unaffected by the first one's refusal; the two lag policies as a fold with both arms and the typed count a hotplug close carries, which is the one decision no fixture can force; the fake's watch corrected to honour the deadline its trait declares — woken by a Condvar a scripted fault ends, so a test never waits out a duration and the daemon's watch loop is not a spin; the hotplug watch's own two failure directions, both of them reachable only because the fake's exhaustive fault menu grew the variants for them — a host that cannot give a watch out refusing the subscribe call with a D13 code before the accept, which is the one moment a subscription can still carry one and the whole reason the watch is started lazily, and a watch that stops under an open subscription ending that subscriber's stream with a named reason rather than leaving it accepted, counted and silently blind for the life of the process (rubric A4, note N59) — watched red against an arm that only cleared its flag, which becomes a named TIMEOUT because that is what a stranded subscriber looks like from outside; the watch thread's own lifecycle, started by the first subscriber and put down after the last one leaves and taken up again by the next, which is the one thing limits::HOTPLUG_WATCH_DEADLINE_MS participates in — no fault is scripted after the last unsubscribe on purpose, so the thread's turn comes from that deadline and from nothing else, and an hour-long one is a named TIMEOUT (measured); a client that floods one WebSocket connection with waiting captures behind a camera a sweep is provably holding, bounded at limits::CAMERA_ENQUEUE_WAITERS permits and refused past it with the same Busy the flag already promises — the bound this transport removed and note N56 wrongly claimed the connection count still supplied, watched red at 36 parked where 32 is the bound; and the hostile directions a client can take, one test apiece and every one of them closing with the same question — a client that subscribes to everything this daemon offers and then vanishes, whose slots come back and whose watch a second client can still use; a session named at subscribe time proven not to be a filter, because the wire carries no such parameter and a client that believed it had one would drop other sessions' events unknowingly, with the session-shaped refusal where it belongs, on the sweep, and the stream neither closed nor fed a phantom event by it; one client watching one sweep twice, told twice under two ids on one connection; a subscription outliving the session it watched and carrying the next one's failure as an event whose discriminant is the one its caller was refused with, because a terminal event is terminal for a control and never for a stream; It also closes the hole an address that is loopback and does not say so: `Ipv6Addr::is_loopback` answers false for `::ffff:127.0.0.1`, the form a dual-stack listener sees for every IPv4 client, so the mapping is unwrapped before the question is asked, the whole of `127.0.0.0/8` is asked rather than `127.0.0.1`, all three wildcard binds are asserted **not** loopback including the mapped one, and the deprecated IPv4-compatible form is deliberately left where the kernel has it (note **N80**). the per-run bearer token D11 asks for, treated as what it is — a secret this process mints, and therefore a secret this process can leak (design D11, docs/7 P5a). 32 bytes of `getrandom(2)` through rustix's `rand` feature rendered as 64 lowercase hex digits; two tokens minted in one process asserted to **differ**, which is the one property that makes it a secret rather than a password and the one a generator seeded from a pid or a start-of-process clock fails while passing everything else in the module; and the kernel-fill loop's property asserted where its branches cannot be, since the syscall is not a seam — over sixteen tokens no position may be a zero digit in all of them, which is what a partially filled buffer looks like. The confinement is asserted rather than asserted-about: the hand-written `Debug` does not contain the token and does say it is hiding something, and the same test reads the secret back through a rendering that is *not* the accessor it was read out of, so a `Token` that had quietly stopped yielding its secret fails here as well as in a browser. `verify` is driven at every shape a rewrite gets wrong first — a prefix, a suffix, an equal-length near miss, a case variant, and nothing at all — and the row is careful about what that is worth: **nothing in this suite can go red on the timing property itself**, because what a test can see is the answer and the claim is about the clock. The shape that argument stands on is `token-comparison-has-one-home.sh`'s row below, and the residual it leaves is note **N78**'s

the token gate's policy over values — which parts of a request may carry a credential, and what it means when more than one does (note **N74**, docs/7 P5a). The rule is that **every credential the request presents must verify, and it must present at least one**, and the three cases that tell it apart from the two gates this project refused to build are each asserted with the refused gate named in the failure message: a good header beside a bad query parameter, a repeated token parameter with the good copy first, and the same repeated with the good copy last — a first-wins gate serves the second, a last-wins gate serves the third, and the difference is reachable by anybody who can get one more parameter appended to a URL an operator is about to open. Two `Authorization` headers is the same rule again, because that is well-formed HTTP and `HeaderMap::get` would answer only the first of them. Beside those: an `Authorization` that is not a bearer credential counted as a credential that *failed* rather than as no credential at all, so a `Basic` header beside a good query parameter is refused by the rule rather than admitted down another path; the scheme compared case-insensitively as RFC 9110 requires and the token not, since it is hex this daemon minted lowercase; the grammar's extra spaces after the scheme allowed and a trailing one refused; a token parameter with no value at all treated as a credential that fails rather than as a request that presented nothing, which is what a URL truncated at its equals sign should meet; whole-name comparison, so a parameter that merely contains the name is somebody else's; and a percent-encoded token refused rather than decoded, so the secret has exactly one spelling. All of it takes a `HeaderMap` and a query string rather than a `Request`, so none of it needs a socket, a router or a runtime — the wire half is `binary(http)`'s row, and neither row is the other's rehearsal

the composition the listener performs, at the seams the integration suite cannot reach (docs/7 P5a). **A posture and a token that disagree are refused, in both directions**: a token-requiring posture with nothing minted is a gate with nothing to check, and a token-less posture with a token minted is a secret printed in a URL and never checked — both refused rather than resolved, because both resolutions are a socket onto a camera somebody did not mean to open, and with the two *agreeing* arrangements asserted to get a router, which is what makes the first two assertions about the disagreement rather than about a function that refuses everything. Then the one transformation between an HTTP path and an asset — the single leading slash stripped, the empty remainder read as the index page, and the name of that page owned by the asset crate rather than spelled here — with a parent-directory traversal, a doubled slash, a trailing slash and a path carrying no leading slash all answering nothing, not because a check catches a traversal but because the table of names is fixed at compile time and there is nothing to traverse (note **N77**). And `open` driven end to end on an ephemeral port for D11's "report the bound port": the URL carries the port the kernel gave and never the zero that was asked for, the token-less cell's URL carries no token parameter at all because an empty one reads as a token that failed to render, and both tests end by cancelling and joining rather than dropping the handle — which is exactly the detached task `Serving`'s `#[must_use]` message is about

docs/9's **Token enforcement** row, over a real TCP socket, a real axum server and a hand-written HTTP client — docs/7 P5a's "401-without/200-with" and "one test per matrix cell", which are one suite because the second is what stops the first being a claim about one cell. The credential every test presents is parsed out of `Serving::ready_to_open_url`, the line an operator copies, rather than read off the `Token` value: a build that published one secret and checked another would otherwise pass this whole suite, and that is the one bug a 401-without/200-with pair exists to be unable to survive. Both forms are driven, because they are two mechanisms a build can lose one at a time — the `Authorization` header, which is what code sends, and the query parameter, which is what a *navigation* can carry and therefore what an operator's first request is. All four cells are here: the two loopback ones through `http::open`, the function `webcam-handler-daemon`'s composition root actually calls, and the two non-loopback ones through `http::serve` with a posture decided about `192.168.1.10:8080` and `0.0.0.0:8080` while the socket stays on loopback — the only way to reach them on a machine with one interface, and they establish that the gate is installed **because the posture said so** and nothing whatever about where the posture came from, which the suite's header states rather than leaves to be inferred. The refusal is asserted as three claims that do not imply one another — the status a client branches on, RFC 6750's challenge, and the body compared against the daemon's own constant, so a build that started answering with a stack trace or with the token fails here rather than in a review — and a path this build does not serve is asserted **401 while anonymous and 404 with the token**, which is the property that says the gate sits outside the router rather than inside it, and is why a stranger cannot map this daemon's surface by watching which paths answer differently (note **N75**). The token-less cell's claim is stronger than "a request with no token is served": no gate is installed at all, the URL the daemon published carries no token to leak, and the 404 still happens, so that cell removes the gate and not the router. Finally the printed URL is taken apart and **opened** rather than matched against a pattern, and the listener is stopped the way the daemon stops it, with the port asserted to refuse a connection afterwards

D11's "TCP is **opt-in**" at the surface where it is opt-in, and the half `crates/daemon/tests/http.rs` says out loud it cannot establish — that the composition root decides its posture from the right two values (docs/7 P5a). `--http` absent parses to `None`, which is neither a default address nor a disabled listener but the branch in `run` that opens no socket and mints no token: a flag that quietly acquired a `default_value` would put a TCP socket on every `webcam-handler-daemon` on the machine while passing every other test in the file. `--http` alone takes D11's `127.0.0.1:0`, with the port asserted to be the kernel's to pick, and is asserted **not** to eat the flag that follows it, which is what an optional value would otherwise do to a command line. A host **name** is refused by the parser rather than resolved, because how far a bind reaches is what decides whether a token is required and a name with several addresses behind it is a name with several answers to that question. the client's files as bytes inside the binary that serves them (design §2.7's "no build step, no npm, no CDN (assets embed; external fetches would violate both the offline posture and the license inventory)", docs/7 P5a's "rust-embed asset serving skeleton"). **`debug-embed` is asserted rather than merely configured** (note **N77**): every embedded asset's bytes are `Cow::Borrowed`, which is a slice of the binary, and the assertion walks every asset rather than sampling one because the feature is per-build — without it a debug `webcam-handler-daemon` reads its asset directory off the filesystem at the absolute path this crate was compiled from, which works on the machine that built it, serves nothing anywhere else, and means the daemon's whole HTTP suite exercises a *different mechanism* from the one a release binary ships. docs/7 P5b's first sentence — "the WS endpoint speaking the same JSON-RPC (the T5 trait has one home; WS is a transport)" — turned into something that can stop being true (design **D10**, **D11**). The suite runs a real `Wchd` over the fake, opens the web listener over the **same `Methods` value** the Unix socket is serving, and drives a real WebSocket upgrade on a real TCP socket. The one-home claim is made two ways because neither implies the other: the same call answered over both transports and compared **as values** (`wch_list`, which reaches the backend, and `wch_controls`, which carries a named parameter and therefore also says the two transports decode parameters alike — one of them arrived through axum's router and the other did not); and **every name the registration carries** named over the WebSocket, with the population read off `Methods::method_names()` and the failure being `-32601`, which is the only answer a second and smaller registration behind that route could give. The count the walk runs over is itself derived, from `daemon::server::ROUTED` plus `routed_subscriptions()`, so a twentieth method or a third subscription lands here as a failure rather than as a silence. Beside those: the gate on an **upgrade**, where an anonymous handshake and an equal-length one-digit-different token are both `401` and the token the daemon printed is a WebSocket, taken out of `ready_to_open_url` rather than off the `Token` value; **subscriptions really delivering** over this transport, which is a promise of jsonrpsee's rather than of ours (its HTTP path builds `OnlyCalls` and answers `-32603`) and is therefore asserted with a real sweep put on the wire unanswered, its typed progress events read as they interleave with the answer, and the session found on disk afterwards through the function the daemon answers `calibrate_list` from; the same three typed D13 refusals over all three transports, so a WebSocket route that had grown a refusal vocabulary of its own fails here rather than in a browser; and the per-connection subscription bound. What the suite does **not** claim is depth per verb — that is `read_verbs.rs`, `mutating_verbs.rs` and `calibrate_verbs.rs`, over the same daemon — and its header says so

the two values `daemon::http::rpc` owns, at the altitude a socket cannot reach (docs/7 P5b). **The credential is taken off the request target before the wire surface is handed it**, and that is a defect class rather than tidiness: jsonrpsee's service logs the whole `http::Request` at `TRACE` on its own target, request line included, so a `RUST_LOG=trace` daemon would have written the bearer token into a journal — a leak the Unix socket cannot have, because its request target is `/`. The stripping happens **after** the gate has read the query (the gate is a layer over the whole router) and before the service sees it, and the test asserts the *string*: three shapes a client sends the token in, each rewritten to a target that does not contain the secret. Both of the function's `None` answers are asserted as the different facts they are — a target with no query at all, which is every request the page's own code makes with an `Authorization` header and where a rewrite would be a copy for nothing; and the **authority-form** request line `CONNECT host:443`, for which `Uri::path` answers the empty string and the empty string is not a URI, so there is nothing to rebuild and equally nothing to strip. That second arm is asserted to be reachable rather than argued: the test pins that `""` still fails to parse, so the day it stops failing the arm says its subject has moved instead of quietly passing. And the endpoint's path is asserted to be a **path** — three readers have to agree on `RPC_PATH` (the route, the suite, and P5c's client, which builds `ws://…/rpc?token=…` from the URL it was opened at), and a value that stopped being one would register a route axum never matches, which is a listener that answers 404 to its own client

**the route P5b added did not acquire an exception to D11**, asserted at the two altitudes that see different things — which is why this row spans two files rather than sitting inside either. AGENTS is explicit that "the web listener is opt-in, loopback + token by default … Weakening either is an owner decision, not a convenience fix", and since the owner's 2026-08-12 ruling narrowed the gate onto the two camera-bearing routes (note **N82**) the cheapest way to weaken it is no longer hypothetical: it is a third route merged after the `route_layer` line, or a route left off `daemon::http::CAMERA_BEARING_PATHS`. Both of those are `web-routes-are-gated.sh`'s; what *this* row holds is that the route which exists is still behind the credential. Over a **real handshake** that is a status and nothing else, because soketto reports a refused upgrade as `Rejected { status_code }`: anonymous is `401`, an equal-length one-digit-different token is `401`, and the token the daemon published opens a socket that answers `wch_list` — the third being what makes the first two about the digits rather than about a route that refuses everything. Over the **HTTP client** on the same path the answer is the refusal in full, and the three claims it carries do not imply one another: the status a client branches on, RFC 6750's challenge, and the body compared against `gate::REFUSAL` so that a build which started answering with a stack trace or with the token fails here rather than in a review. The same test pins that an authenticated `GET` of that path is **405 and not 404** — two facts at once, that the request got past the gate and that `/rpc` is a route rather than a name the asset fallback failed to find, since "POST is required" is an answer only the wire surface gives — and, in the same run against the same listener, that the page beside it is served to a request presenting **nothing**, which is the half of the ruling a build can get wrong in the opposite direction. A build that registered the endpoint on some other path answers 404 there, from the asset table, and now does it with no 401 in front of it

`limits::RPC_MAX_SUBSCRIPTIONS_PER_CONNECTION` **read rather than transcribed, on both transports that serve the wire surface** (AGENTS's "bounded everything", note **N38**, docs/7 P5b). The bound has one home in `schema::limits` and, since P5b, one reader in `daemon::server::wire_bounds` — the single `ServerConfig` both `daemon::uds` and `daemon::http::rpc` build their jsonrpsee service from, because two copies of that expression would be two answers to "how many streams may one connection open" and the second copy is the one that stops matching the day the constant moves. This row is the thing that can go red on it: the same experiment runs over `AF_UNIX` and over a browser-shaped TCP WebSocket, and a web listener that had quietly inherited jsonrpsee's own defaults would let 1024 subscriptions onto one connection and fail at the ninth. The refusal is asserted as a **`-32006` answer to the subscribe call**, before any handler runs, which is what makes connect-and-abandon cost a client its own slots and nobody else's — and -32006 is jsonrpsee's own code, with D13's block starting at -32012 (`api::codes`), so there is no collision to reason about. Each arm ends by showing that a **second** connection is unaffected, which is the half that says the bound is per connection rather than per daemon — and on the TCP side that the `ConnectionGuard` the same builder hands out did not refuse it either, since that guard is per builder and this transport has one of its own — and that both connections still answer a verb, so the refusal cost one subscription and neither client a socket

**a stopping daemon ends an open stream with a reason rather than with a closed socket, on the browser's transport as well as on `webcam-handler-client`'s** (AGENTS: open streams are "cancelled, never awaited, on shutdown"; `daemon::shutdown`'s step 3 before its step 4; docs/7 P5b). The half that costs something is the payload: a listener that simply stopped would end these streams too — with nothing at all, indistinguishable from the daemon crashing or the machine losing its network — so both arms assert the typed `daemon::events::SHUTTING_DOWN` arriving as jsonrpsee's `subscription_error` notification, matched **by subscription id**, and then assert the live subscriber count coming back to zero, which is what makes the ending the end of the subscription rather than one message on a stream still holding a task and a receiver. The TCP arm is also where the *timing* of the WebSocket transport's stop is pinned. An upgraded connection stops belonging to axum the moment hyper hands the socket over, so `axum::serve`'s graceful shutdown neither waits for it nor closes it; what closes it is jsonrpsee's `ServerHandle`, and `daemon::http::Serving::stopped` asks for it at the **join** rather than wiring it to the cancellation — because cancelling the token and stopping the transport in the same instant is a race the reason loses, which is the measurement `daemon::shutdown`'s header records for the other transport (`tests/signals.rs` saw the ending about half the time without the wait). A build that stopped the two together fails here on the read, finding a closed socket where a payload should be

docs/7 P5b's **"a test client reads N multipart frames"**, over a real TCP socket, a real axum server and a real camera actor (design §2.6's "the MJPEG preview route (`multipart/x-mixed-replace`, fed from the actor's latest-frame watch channel)"). The client is hand-written for `support/tcp.rs`'s reason and one more of its own: this response has no length and no end until somebody causes one, so a client that read to end-of-file could not read it at all — and it decodes HTTP/1.1's **chunked** framing, because a body with no length is chunked and a suite that skipped that layer would be asserting about a stream it had not actually parsed. Every field of every part is read rather than counted: the delimiter with its two leading hyphens, `Content-Type: image/jpeg`, a `Content-Length` that has to agree with the payload that follows it (which is what lets a conforming reader take a frame without scanning it for the boundary), the blank line, and the CRLF between the frame and the next delimiter. "Successive" is asserted as a property of **two** numbers rather than as a count of parts, because a build that published one frame forever would deliver the same bytes eight times and pass any assertion that only counted: the publication index must advance, which says this daemon published eight distinct frames, and the driver's own sequence number must advance, which says the *device* delivered eight rather than one buffer handed out repeatedly. The bytes are checked to be a JPEG at both ends (SOI and EOI) — legitimate here only because the frames are the fake's synthetic pattern, and the weakest thing worth asserting: not what the picture is, only that a build which skipped `engine::preview::start`'s negotiation check has not put a YUYV buffer in an `image/jpeg` part. Beside the framing, D12's lifecycle from the other end: one `open`, one `STREAMON` and one feed, each read off the fake's own counters against a baseline the fixture asserted was zero, so the camera was opened by *this* rather than by something the fixture did

docs/7 P5b's **stalled-reader** criterion — the one that says **drop** rather than **backpressure**, which is design D12's "a slow HTTP consumer drops frames and never backpressures the device" turned into something that can stop being true. Three numbers make it and **none of them is inferred**: the daemon's published count, a `watch` this test *awaits* rather than polls (`Wchd::watch_preview_frames`), which advances while the client reads nothing; the client's own count of parts, which is a local variable in the test and stays at one; and the gap the client then reads off the wire — successive parts whose `X-Wch-Frame-Index` headers jump — with the daemon's skipped count (`Wchd::watch_preview_drops`) asserted to have counted at least that many, which is rubric rule 3's "dropped, and counted" at the far end of the same fact. The stall is made **deterministic without a clock**, which is the part that is easy to get wrong: the client connects through a socket whose receive buffer it set small and the daemon's listener is bound through one whose send buffer is small (Linux gives an accepted socket the listener's `SO_SNDBUF`), so "this reader has stopped" reaches the daemon within a handful of frames instead of within however much `net.ipv4.tcp_wmem` felt like buffering on the machine that ran the test. Nothing sleeps: the wait ends on a `watch` change, and the search for the gap is a **bounded** loop, so a build that delivered everything fails on an assertion rather than reading forever. A queue in place of the latest-frame `watch` fails this in whichever way it was built — an unbounded one keeps every frame for the reader, so the indices come back contiguous and the skipped count never moves; a bounded one stops the *capture* when the reader stops, so the published count never advances and the wait never ends, which `.config/nextest.toml`'s deadline turns into a named failure carrying this test's name rather than a hang

docs/7 P5b's **compression-exclusion** criterion, and it is two assertions in one test because either alone proves nothing. `tower-http`'s `CompressionLayer` arrives with this sub-milestone (design §2.8 lists it for the daemon and P5a's manifest comment named the preview route as the reason it was not there yet), so the test asserts on the same listener, with the same `Accept-Encoding: gzip`, that **the assets come back `Content-Encoding: gzip`** — without which "the preview is uncompressed" would be satisfied by a build that had no compression at all, which is the greenest a test of an exclusion can be while checking nothing — and that **the preview response carries no `Content-Encoding` at all**. It is not left at the absence of a header: the first part's payload is asserted to be a JPEG on the wire, SOI to EOI, which a reader gets only if nothing re-encoded the stream between the camera and the socket. The exclusion it checks is **structural rather than configured**: `daemon::http::listener::router` applies the layer and merges the preview route afterwards, so there is no predicate to invert and no content-type list to keep current — and it has to be structural, because `CompressionLayer`'s own default predicate declines `image/*` and `multipart/x-mixed-replace` is not `image/*`, so leaving the decision to a default is leaving it to the wrong answer. What compressing this route would cost is not bytes: a compressing middleware buffers, and what it would be buffering is the part boundary a browser's `` repaints on

design §2.6's **"an open MJPEG tab must not hang shutdown"**, as a number rather than a paragraph (AGENTS: open streams are "cancelled, never awaited, on shutdown"; docs/7 P5b). The tab is provably open *and provably stalled*, which is the case the requirement is really about and the one a comfortable test misses: a reader that is still draining its socket ends by itself the moment its feed is withdrawn, so a build whose response body ignored the cancellation would pass a test written that way and hang in front of a browser that had been minimised. This one reads a frame, stops, and waits — on the daemon's published count, not on a clock — until far more frames exist than the deliberately small socket buffers on both ends can hold, at which point the writer is parked in a send that only the cancellation can end. **What it found is that ending the body is necessary and not sufficient**, and that is the sub-milestone's one discovery about a claim the design had already made: ending a body leaves hyper a final chunk to *write*, a client with a full socket cannot be written to, and `axum::serve`'s graceful shutdown waits for the connection — so `webcam-handler-daemon` stopped when somebody scrolled a tab back into view. Meeting the requirement therefore takes two things, and both are asserted here: `daemon::http::preview`'s writer watching the same token on **both** places it can wait (for a frame, and for room in its channel), and a **bound on the join** — `limits::WEB_LISTENER_STOP_MS`, after which `daemon::http::Serving::stopped` aborts the listener task and says so at `warn`, which is AGENTS' "cancelled, never awaited" rather than a concession to it. The outer bound the test asserts against is `limits::DAEMON_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_MS` and it is **asserted** rather than left to the runner, because the difference between "this test failed" and "this run timed out" is the difference between a diagnosis and a mystery. Then the client's own end of the same fact: the bytes the kernel had already buffered arrive and the connection reaches end-of-file, which is a listener that closed a socket rather than one that walked away from it

the four claims P5b's preview owes that are not about frames arriving: **exclusivity, the gate, the refusals, and the cost** (design **D12**, **D11**; the owner's 2026-08-12 ruling). *One streamer, whatever the tab count*: two readers of one camera are one `open`, one `STREAMON` and one feed — read off the fake's own counters — and both are served real frames, which is what says the second tab **joined** a stream rather than being refused one; then the first tab closes and the second keeps painting, so the capture belongs to the feed rather than to whichever reader started it; then the last one closes and the feed is retired, awaited on `Wchd::watch_previewed_cameras` because "the last tab left" is an event, with the stream asserted **not** to have been restarted on its way out. *The gate*, and since the owner's 2026-08-12 ruling this is the row's load-bearing member rather than a belt beside braces: the gate used to be one `Router::layer` over one router and is now a `route_layer` over the routes, so "the camera is behind the token" is a property of a **list** — `daemon::http::CAMERA_BEARING_PATHS` — and a list can be wrong (note **N82**). The population is read off that list rather than written in the test, and each path is driven four ways because none of the four implies the others: a request presenting nothing is `401` with RFC 6750's challenge; an equal-length one-digit-different token is `401` in **both** credential forms, so the gate is comparing rather than looking for a parameter; the real token gets past to an answer that is neither the gate's `401` nor the asset table's `404`, which is what catches a path that is on the list and is not a route at all; and the population is asserted non-empty, because every claim above quantifies over it. Then the other half of the same ruling, in the same run against the same listener: `GET /` presenting nothing is the page, so a build that put the gate back over everything fails here rather than looking stricter than it was asked to be. What this row cannot see is a route nobody named — a test can only drive the paths somebody wrote down — and that is `scripts/gates/web-routes-are-gated.sh`'s row, one line down. *The refusals*, at both arms of the two-status projection an `` can act on: `404` for a name no camera answers to and `400` for a request that named none, with **no camera opened** in either case, which is the half that says the refusal happened before the device rather than by a stream that started and stopped. *The cost* was the fourth member of this row until the owner ruled it away (2026-08-12, note **N83**): a `wch_photo` taken while a preview held the stream met `Busy` from the device, `a_photo_while_a_preview_is_running_is_refused_by_the_device_and_the_preview_survives` pinned it, and it went red on purpose the day the mechanism landed. It is not a claim this row lost — it is four claims this gate gained, on the rows below, and the reason its name is written here rather than deleted is that a row which quietly shrinks is how a suite stops proving what its `what` column says

the three halves of the preview that are assertable **without a socket, a camera or a browser** — the altitude the integration suite above cannot reach, and where the decisions actually live (docs/7 P5b). In `engine::preview`, the loop's shape: the stream is started **once** and each command takes one frame off it, asserted by the frames' sequence numbers advancing across separate calls (a build that restarted the stream per frame would meet the fake's `Busy` on the second `STREAMON`, which is V4L2's own rule); a sink that has stopped watching is what ends the capture, since the sink is the only thing that can see a socket; a frame that did not arrive is an **idle turn and not a failure**, while a device that went away is refused in its own words, which is the conversion AGENTS rule 7 forbids, caught in the one place it would happen; and a negotiation a browser cannot render is refused with the stream stopped, both directions, because D5 lets a driver answer with a format nobody asked for and this is the one caller that cannot pass that difference on. In `daemon::preview`, the channel property itself: a reader that missed frames is handed the **newest** one and the gap is counted, which is what a `watch` does and no queue does; a frame over `limits::PREVIEW_MAX_FRAME_BYTES` is dropped and counted rather than held, because `bytesused` is the driver's number and a daemon that allocated whatever it was told to would let a device decide how much memory it uses (design §2.5); the two ways to say "enough" — no readers, and a cancelled daemon — asserted separately, because they are two mechanisms and a build that read only one of them holds a camera open for the case it does not read; a withdrawn feed ending its readers' streams rather than leaving them waiting; and `limits::PREVIEW_MAX_VIEWERS_PER_CAMERA` refusing the fifth reader with `Busy` and admitting one again when a place comes free, so the bound is a bound rather than a latch. In `daemon::http::preview`, the wire's own shapes: one multipart part asserted **as bytes**, since every line of it is load-bearing for a client this project does not control; the camera parameter read out of a query string and percent-decoded, where the credential deliberately is not, with the contrast argued at both sites; a percent escape that is not one left where it was written, so this decoder holds no opinion about D1's grammar; and the two statuses, each driven with a refusal that really occurs on this path

**the structural half of what replaced a property the owner's 2026-08-12 ruling took away** (note **N82**). Until that ruling "every route the web listener serves is behind D11's token" was true by construction — `Router::layer` wrapped the routes, the fallback router and the catch-all, so a request could not reach a handler without meeting the gate. The assets are now served without authentication and the gate is a `route_layer` over the routes, so which paths are gated is a *decision* where it used to be a shape, and a camera-bearing route added later without being named is a live camera served to strangers — green in this workspace, because a test can only ask for a path somebody named (`kill-is-never-a-fallback.sh`'s argument about an absence, one transport along). Four claims: `daemon::http::CAMERA_BEARING_PATHS` exists, is non-empty and names **constants** rather than literals, each declared in the daemon's `http` tree; every `.route(`/`.route_service(`/`.nest(`/`.nest_service(` in the workspace's product code passes one of those constants from inside those modules; `.fallback(`/`.fallback_service(` appears exactly once, in the composition, naming the asset handler — the door the route claim does not watch, since a fallback is precisely what this listener now serves *without* a credential; and the composition still installs `gate::check` exactly once with exactly one `route_layer(`, because every claim above is true both of a tree that stopped gating anything and of a tree that put the gate back over everything. Its honest limit is in its own header: it checks shape, so a route registered *after* the `route_layer` line satisfies every claim here and is caught by the behavioural row above instead — the two are only worth having together. Eighteen fail arms and five green ones, `pass_case_a_test_may_build_a_router_of_its_own` among them

**the ruling as a requirement rather than a permission**: the client's own files are served to a request presenting nothing (owner ruling, 2026-08-12; D11's amendment; note **N82**), so a build that kept the token over `/index.html` is red here. Three answers to one anonymous client, and a build can get any of them wrong on its own: an asset is `200`, a path that names no asset is `404` — which used to be a `401` and is the visible half of the property note N75 gave up — and every path on `daemon::http::CAMERA_BEARING_PATHS` is `401` in full. The second test walks the population `webcam-handler-web`'s own table reports rather than a list written here, so P5c's ES modules join it by existing, which is the only arrangement in which "the client loads with no credential" keeps meaning what it means today: a module graph is one request per module and one `401` in it is a client that does not run (note **N76**, retired by this ruling)

docs/9's "Token enforcement" pair at the address the 2026-08-12 ruling moved it to: the credential is asserted **on the routes that carry or drive the camera**, because a credential presented to an ungated path proves nothing about a gate. Both forms, because they are two mechanisms a build can lose one at a time — the `Authorization` header is what the page's own `fetch` and its `` send, and `?token=` is what a URL can carry, which is all a `new WebSocket(url)` has (note **N74**). "Past the gate" is asserted as an answer only the route behind it gives — jsonrpsee's `405` to a `GET` that is not an upgrade, the preview's `400` to a request naming no camera — so neither is reachable through the refusal and neither is the asset table's `404`. The near-miss half drives an equal-length one-digit-different token and a **prefix** against both gated routes in both forms, the prefix because a gate comparing with `starts_with` instead of `Token::verify` serves it while refusing every equal-length candidate; and the token they are near misses of still gets past, so the refusals are about the digits rather than about a route that refuses everybody

`Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` on every response the web listener writes (D11's 2026-08-12 amendment). The token rides the document's URL, so the URL a browser holds for this page **is** the key to a camera and a `Referer` header is that URL handed to whatever the page links out to; same-origin leakage back to the daemon is harmless, a link out is not, and the page P5a ships has no links while P5c's may — which is the wrong order in which to discover a header. **the suspend/resume sequence is one operation, and it is exact** (design **D12**'s 2026-08-12 amendment; note **N83**). The owner ruled that a photo taken while somebody is watching a preview stops that stream, takes its frame and starts it again rather than being refused `Busy` — and the whole of the mechanism is `engine::preview::while_suspended`, which has no public `suspend` and no public `resume` because a suspend a caller can invoke on its own is one somebody forgets to resume. Three claims here and none implies the others. *The sequence happens*, with a real `engine::capture::grab` inside it rather than a stand-in — which matters because what a photo actually does is start a stream of its own, and the scriptable double refuses a second `STREAMON` exactly as V4L2 does, so a build that skipped the suspend fails here with `Busy` rather than passing a test that only counted stops; the counts are asserted on both sides (three starts, two stops) so a resume that ran twice or not at all is a different pair of numbers. *The resume is exact*: it asks for the stream that was **negotiated**, field for field, rather than re-issuing the preview's own request — D5 lets a driver answer with something other than what was asked for, so on a camera whose preview was adjusted those are different asks and the difference is a picture that changes size underneath a page that has already sized an `` around it. *A capture with no preview touches no stream at all*: the early return is the work with nothing before or after it, so "a photo with no preview running is unchanged" is a property of the code path rather than of a test that happened to check the observable parts — and the numbers are exactly what a build that took the suspend path anyway would move, because the stop is harmless and the start that followed it would leave the camera streaming for nobody

**the stream comes back on every path out of the capture, and the pause is bounded** (AGENTS rule 8; `limits::PREVIEW_SUSPEND_MAX_MS`; note **N83**). A photo that errored and left the preview dead would be "leave the camera as you found it" broken by the code that exists to honour it, so this row drives the three ways the work can end and the one way it can be refused before it starts. *The error path*: the work's refusal travels unchanged and the stream is running again before the caller sees it. *The panic path*, which is why the resume is a drop guard rather than a line at the end of a function — the most popular V4L2 crate panics on a control type this kernel emits \[PF:1\], so "the backend panicked" is a measured failure mode and a preview that ended because somebody pressed a photo button would be indistinguishable from a camera that failed. *A resume the device itself refuses*, which is the failure with no good answer given the least bad one: the photo is not thrown away (the frame is gone and cannot be retaken) and the refusal is not swallowed (it rides in `Gap::resumed`, where the daemon counts it, logs it, and the feed's own driver ends the stream on its next turn) — asserted as both halves, because a build that returned the resume's error instead would pass any test that only checked that something failed. *The bound, in both directions*: a settle budget past `PREVIEW_SUSPEND_MAX_MS` is refused **before** the stream is stopped, so a request too expensive to serve costs the viewers nothing — and a budget exactly at it is served, which is what makes the refusal about the number rather than about a function that refuses everything. The bound is checked against the caller's declared budget rather than measured afterwards because nothing can interrupt a `DQBUF` the actor's thread is already inside; a limit consulted after the work would be a number in a log wearing a bound's name

**the verb that carries the mechanism, over the fake replaying a committed profile** (design **D6**, **D12**; note **N83**). The sequence lives inside `engine::photo::take` rather than beside it, which is what makes `webcam-handler-cli`, `webcam-handler-daemon` and any later caller get it without arranging anything (§2.10: one home per law) — and this row is that placement, asserted through the verb rather than through the helper. Three claims. *The photo happens during a live stream and is still verbatim*: a suspend/resume that re-negotiated into a format needing a re-encode would leave the picture intact and cost the product what AGENTS calls it ("verbatim camera JPEG when the sink allows — byte fidelity is the product"), so `Rendering::is_verbatim` is asserted beside the three `STREAMON`s the sequence costs. *What a viewer sees is a fact rather than a paragraph*: the resumed stream's first frame is **sequence 0 again**, because `STREAMON` resets the driver's counter — the one signal on the wire that says "this stream restarted" rather than "frames were dropped", which move the number forward — and it is passed through as the device reported it, since that field's contract is that it is the device's number (D5). *The bound reaches the request*: the number checked is the settle deadline the `PhotoRequest` carries, so this is where `limits::PREVIEW_SUSPEND_MAX_MS` and a client's own ask meet, refused with the preview left streaming and served again one millisecond lower. The no-preview arm is the conditional half: one stream, no gap, and the camera not left streaming — the numbers a build that suspended unconditionally would move

**the ruling over a real socket, and the pause counted rather than silent** (owner ruling, 2026-08-12; note **N83**; rubric rule 3). These four replace the row member that pinned the old `Busy` and went red on purpose. *A photo during a preview*: the answer is a photo whose bytes are still a JPEG bitstream and whose `byte_count` agrees with them (note N34's predicate, from the client's end), the interruption count is **read** off `Wchd::watch_preview_interruptions` rather than inferred, frames are published after the answer that did not exist before it — awaited on the daemon's own count with `PREVIEW_FRAME_WAIT_MS * 2` around it, so a build that skipped the resume fails on an assertion naming the bound instead of hanging — and the fake's counters say one descriptor and exactly three streams: the preview's, the photo's own, and the resume. *A photo with no preview* answers exactly as it did before the ruling: one stream, no interruption, no feed. *A capture that fails mid-photo* still leaves the preview streaming and **still counts the interruption**, which is the case a gap counted only on success would under-report and the reason `engine::photo::Taken` carries the gap beside the outcome; the failure is a settle deadline of zero rather than a queued frame fault, because while a preview is running there is a `next_frame` in flight continuously and a frame fault would be a race between the preview's turn and the photo's capture — the fault-menu injection lives in the engine suite where the double is exclusive. *Two tabs with a photo between them* are still one streamer: neither tab is told anything, both keep painting, one `open`, one feed, three streams. *Two photos at once* is the shape that reaches the one window the whole design is about: the suspend, the capture and the resume are indivisible because they are one actor command on the thread that owns the device, and a build that split them across two commands puts the second photo's `STREAMON` between the first's stop and its restart — so one of the two meets `Busy`, and no other test in this suite has two requests in flight to notice. Both answers are checked, the interruption count is two, and five streams is one capture and one resume each on top of the preview's. The count is what makes the pause observable at all: nothing is published during it, so nothing is dropped, and `watch_preview_frames` and `watch_preview_drops` are both blind to it
