**the structural half of docs/7 P6a's re-parse requirement, and the one criterion in this phase that exists because a test cannot be written for it** (AGENTS rule 1). P6a asks the muxer's output to be checked by "an independent re-parse path that is **not** the writer's code", and `crates/imaging/src/avi.rs`'s module doc makes the claim in the strongest form there is — the reader and the muxer "share **no** code, not a constant, not a FourCC, not a helper". The row above is the behavioural half and it cannot hold this: `the_size_fields_agree_with_the_bytes_written_over_many_frame_length_sequences` is exactly as green against a re-parse that reads its FourCCs off the muxer's own line as against one derived from the specification — greener, because two sides that share a constant agree by construction — so the day a shared `FOURCC_MOVI` or a `chunk_header()` helper is factored into a third module beside these two, every test in this workspace passes and the property P6a asked for is gone with nothing left to notice. A test sees values; this claim is about `use` statements and where files sit. Four claims, each able to go red on its own: `read.rs` and `write.rs` are both under `crates/imaging/src/avi/` and are the **only** `.rs` files there, because a third module is precisely where a shared layout helper lands and it would satisfy every other claim here; the reader's product code names no path into the writer, however spelled; the writer's product code names no path into the reader, while its `#[cfg(test)]` half may and does and must, since that coupling *is* what P6a asked for and a predicate forbidding it would forbid the criterion above; and both modules are still **declared**, in `avi.rs` and in the crate root, because an orphaned `.rs` file is not a compile error in Rust and a wall whose subject has left the build has stopped being able to fail (`dependency-walls.sh`'s "the crate left the workspace" arm, charged to a module). Populations are derived — the crate's directory from `cargo metadata`, the modules from the directory listing, the declarations spelled from the stems that listing produced — and the crate, the parent module and the two names are asserted to exist before anything is counted. It goes red in the direction of *sharing*, never of drift: it inherits its limit rather than restating it as a strength, and the limit is that it sees imports and file layout and not two implementations that drifted into agreeing by copy-paste, which review carries. Ten fail arms and three green ones, `pass_case_the_muxers_tests_may_drive_the_reader` the one that matters most among them

**the byte-exact fixtures for D7's raw fallback**, and the AVI row above's argument arriving at a container where it is worth more. `crates/imaging/fixtures/y4m/two-frame-64x48-c422.y4m` and `-mono.y4m` are 12 341 and 6 198 bytes, and this test re-emits both: a header field reordered, an `A1:1` pixel aspect that grew back, a per-frame parameter added, a plane written in the wrong order, the two empty chroma planes of a `Cmono` frame silently dropped — each of those changes the bytes and nothing else in the suite is looking at them. What it proves is narrow and `crates/imaging/fixtures/README.md` says so where a human reading the directory will find it: a fixture produced by the code under test proves nothing about correctness, only that the format has not drifted. **The privacy half is where this differs from the AVI row.** An AVI hides its frames inside JPEG bitstreams; a Y4M payload *is* the picture, one 8-bit luma sample per byte in raster order, which is the most direct form a camera frame can take in this repository — so this test re-generates every sample from the three position functions in `imaging::y4m::tests` and compares them against the planes it reads back out of the committed bytes through the independent parser, and `scripts/gates/no-frame-bytes-in-repo.sh` now sniffs the `YUV4MPEG2 ` magic and reads the extent out of the header line (five `fail_case_y4m_*` arms). Two containers arrived invisible to that gate in two consecutive phases, which is the argument for its format list being a decision somebody makes rather than a thing that grows on its own

**the independent re-parse for the second container**, held to the standard docs/7 P6a set for the first: the checking path must not be the writer's code. `imaging::y4m`'s `#[cfg(test)] parse_y4m` is ~90 lines derived from the YUV4MPEG2 format description — it re-derives the plane sizes from the `C` tag it read rather than asking the module for them, and it knows nothing about `MAGIC`, `FRAME_MARKER` or `Layout`. The `y4m` crate's own decoder would **not** have served and that is a measurement rather than a preference (note **N107**): it ships in the same file as the encoder it would have been checking and shares `get_plane_sizes` with it, so it agrees by construction on exactly the questions a re-parse is for. This row drives all three colorspaces — `Cmono`, `C422`, `C420` — through it and compares every plane against samples re-generated from position functions with **disjoint value ranges**, which is load-bearing rather than tidy: note **N108** records a hand-applied mutant that swapped Cb and Cr passing the entire 1261-test workspace suite while the fixtures had neutral chroma. `the_parser_refuses_the_ways_this_writer_could_be_wrong` asserts the parser's own eight refusals first, because a parser that accepts everything proves nothing about what it accepted

**the chroma orientation of the product decode path, which nothing in this workspace asserted until 2026-08-15** — the half note **N108** recorded and deliberately left open at P6b, closed as note **N130**. The row above buys the same property for the *recording* path; this one buys it where a camera's YUYV or NV12 frame becomes a PNG or a re-encoded JPEG, and the reason it needs its own row is that the defect is not detectable by any test this phase already had. Measured rather than argued: `yuyv422_to_rgb` → `yvyu422_to_rgb`, `yuv_nv12_to_rgb` → `yuv_nv21_to_rgb`, and the chroma plane started at `w * h` instead of at `y_stride * h` — three one-identifier edits, each of which is every recorded colour inverted about the neutral axis or read from the wrong offset — each passed **1381 of 1381 tests** and each turns this row red. The expectation is derived from Rec. ITU-R BT.601 and from the two arguments `imaging::decode` actually passes (`YuvRange::Limited`, `YuvStandardMatrix::Bt601`), with the coefficients written as `2(1 - Kr)` and `2·Kr(1 - Kr)/Kg` rather than as decimals, because a fixture whose expectations came out of the implementation cannot catch the implementation being wrong. Two of the five tests are about the **fixture** and not the decoder, and they are in the selection on purpose: the disjoint bands (luma 58–100, Cb 108–126, Cr 140–156) and the position functions are what give the other three any discriminating power at all, so a fixture quietly re-centred on neutral chroma has to be a red row rather than a green one that checks nothing — the P6b defect reintroduced at the fixture level was watched turning five tests red. The property N108 did not name and this row also holds is that the decoded RGB clips at **neither** end in **either** chroma orientation, asserted per pixel, because a channel saturated at 0 or 255 is constant along the dimension under test

**the one cap law, walked across both containers** — what pays for AVI and Y4M counting their own bytes instead of sharing an accounting layer. The two charge for a frame differently (AVI: an eight-byte chunk header, a pad byte, and a sixteen-byte `idx1` entry written at close; Y4M: six bytes of `FRAME\n` and nothing at close), so a shared projection would have to be told about both, which is how one of them quietly stops enforcing a bound. This walks `schema::video::CapReached::ALL` against `schema::video::VideoFormat::ALL` and drives each container to each bound, deriving the size cap from what that container actually charged for one frame rather than from a literal — six pairs, counted, with the walk asserting its own arity so a container or a cap that vanished from a vocabulary cannot empty it. Each arm also asserts the *shape* AGENTS rule 7 requires and not merely the value: the frame inside every bound is `Written`, the frame past it is `Refused(cap)` and nothing after it is written, and `finish` names the bound — because a cap reported as an `Err` would make an agent unable to tell 'your recording is as long as you allowed' from 'your camera is misbehaving'. A hand-applied mutant that stopped counting the `FRAME` marker in the Y4M projection was watched failing it

**docs/7 P6b's MJPG-only muxer policy, stated as a total function rather than as a rule somebody remembers**: 'non-MJPG `record` requests get Y4M or `FormatUnsupported { available }`'. The pairing lives in one place — `schema::video::VideoFormat::carries`, an exhaustive match, so a third container is a compile error rather than a set somebody forgot to extend — and this row is the only thing that can hold it **total**, because it is the only place both vocabularies are visible: D6's closed source-format set is `imaging::decode::SourceFormat` and `webcam-handler-schema` knows nothing about which formats can be decoded. It walks D6's set and asserts each format is carried by **exactly one** container, then walks back the other way and asserts every recordable format is one this build can decode, then asserts the two sets have the same size — three directions, because a pairing that was merely non-empty could still leave a new D6 format recordable by nothing, and the only symptom would be a `FormatUnsupported` on a camera that works. Its sibling `a_container_that_cannot_carry_the_stream_is_refused_before_a_header_is_written` carries the other half: the refusal is `FormatUnsupported` naming what that container *would* have taken, it fires before a byte reaches the sink, and it is never a silent redirect to the other container — a caller who typed `out.avi` over a YUYV camera must not receive a Y4M

**cap enforcement through the executor** (docs/7 P6b's first criterion), which is a different claim from the muxer's own. `imaging::video`'s walk proves each container refuses at each bound; what it cannot see is a `RecordingCaps` this engine assembled out of `schema::limits`, a loop this engine wrote, and an ending this engine reports. So the first of these three is that walk again — `schema::video::CapReached::ALL`, driven through `engine::record::drive` — on a `FrozenClock`, which is note **N60**'s second shape doing exactly what it is for: a deadline that cannot expire makes the *cap* the only reachable ending however loaded the host running it. The second is the duration bound, on a clock whose steps the loop takes rather than the test, because a test that hands a loop a clock and gets an answer back has no moment in which to move one; the frame count is arithmetic rather than approximate, since `drive` reads that clock exactly once per turn. The third is the assertion nothing else in this repository can make: that the loop **stops asking the device** the moment a cap refuses a frame. That is a bug a summary cannot show — the muxer's refusal is sticky, so a take that kept streaming for the eighty-eight seconds after its size cap would write a byte-identical file — and the only observable is how often `next_frame` was called, which is what the counting camera in that suite exists for

**every fault leaves a parseable file** (docs/7 P6b, in those words), and *which* reader gets it. `engine::record::SinkFault` is design §2.9's fault menu for the file seam — a `closed_vocabulary!` walked exhaustively, four variants that each reach a different path through the muxer and leave a different file: none at all, a cut-short `movi` prefix, an empty one, and a whole one whose flush refused. Every arm asserts D13's disk-shaped `StorageIo` naming the caller's own path, because `webcam-handler-imaging` answers `DeviceIo` naming a muxer step — a container has no business knowing what a path is — and an unattended reader handed that for a full disk will go and look at the camera. The two readers are asserted in **both** directions rather than one of them in one: a recording poisoned mid-take has no `idx1`, so `imaging::avi::read::recover_frames` reads it and `read_stream` refuses, and a change that made the truncated file strictly parseable would mean the close had run over a poisoned sink. The device half is the same claim from the other end — a camera unplugged mid-take still gets its index written, so the strict reader accepts *that* file — which is what makes the pair say which failure leaves which file rather than only that something somewhere is readable. The injected `ENOSPC` is the kernel's own number, asked of `/dev/full` rather than believed (note **N10**)

**D7's MJPG-only muxer policy, proven against a device that really cannot do MJPG** — docs/7 P6b: 'non-MJPG `record` requests get Y4M or `FormatUnsupported { available }`'. `imaging::video`'s pairing walk holds the law over the *vocabulary*; this holds it over a *camera*, because `corpus/profiles/chicony-ir.json` is a captured profile of a real GREY-only device and the fake replays it, so all three arms are answers about hardware rather than about a fixture built to make the point. A `.y4m` sink records, and the file's own `FRAME` markers are counted against the summary rather than the summary being taken on trust. A path with **no** extension is answered from the negotiated stream, which is the arm AGENTS' handless primary consumer depends on: an agent that has not enumerated a camera's formats cannot know to type `.y4m`, and a verb where it must is a verb needing a call sequence. And a `.avi` sink is refused with `FormatUnsupported { requested: GREY, available: [MJPG, JPEG] }` — naming what AVI *would* have taken, never quietly redirected to the other container, arriving after the negotiation because the refusal is about it, and leaving the camera not streaming and no file behind

**D10's method list is complete** (docs/7 P6c: "`record_start/stop/status` on the T5 trait — D10 is now complete"), and this is the row that says so where the surface is declared. It reads the spellings off a real `RpcModule` built by the generated `into_rpc()` rather than off a list in the file, because the macro's own registration is the authority on what the wire carries — and it pins the twenty-two names, because a wire name is a compatibility contract in the way a D13 code is and changing one has to be a diff somebody wrote on purpose. What it replaces is the absence assertion the same test used to carry: three names asserted **missing** with the comment "`record_*` join at P6 with their tests". That line was the last thing in this workspace still saying D10 was unfinished, and deleting it rather than relaxing it is the point — a build that lost `wch_record_stop` now fails on the pinned list, where before it would have satisfied an absence

**a recording really reaches the device, and the two counts of it agree** — the claim a status document cannot make about itself. A build whose driver never issued a turn writes a header, closes it, and answers a report whose `frames_written` is zero, which is also what an honest zero-duration take answers; so the discriminating assertion is a non-zero count on *both* sides, the daemon's report and the file read back by `imaging::avi::read::read_stream` — the strict reader P6a wrote from the RIFF/AVI specification before the muxer existed and which shares no code with it. The second test is the cross-check `schema::video::TakeStatus::frames_written` promises in its own doc: a running take's count and the finished `RecordingSummary`'s are the same number arrived at on two sides, the daemon counting what the container **accepted** and the container counting what it wrote — so a build that counted refused frames, or stopped counting, would leave a progress mechanism telling an agent nothing was happening while a file grew. Nothing in either sleeps: `Wchd::watch_finished_recordings` is what says the driver put the take down, because "the take ended" is an event and a test that polled the registry for it would be a test with a sleep in it under another name

**the recording state a socket can ask about, and the two refusals D13's closed eighteen answer it with** (note **N114**). One take per camera: a second `record_start` is `Error::Busy`, which means *retry* to an unattended reader and is the advice that works, since the take that is running is bounded by its own duration — and its `holders` list is **empty**, because the pid holding that camera is this daemon and naming it would invite a client to kill the process it is talking to (`engine::actor` makes the identical choice for the identical reason). A `record_stop` on a camera holding nothing is `Error::IllegalTransition` naming `record_start` in its remedy, deliberately not a bland success: an agent has to be able to tell "my recording is over" from "my `record_start` never took", and those are the same call's two answers. Three slot states are walked in the order a caller meets them — never recorded, recording, ended-and-collected — and the third answers the same as the first, which is a decision rather than an accident: what a caller can do about either is start a recording. The `Busy` is shown to be a state rather than a latch, because the camera records again afterwards

**the four requests only a socket can send, refused before a camera opens — and the one obligation the daemon's file seam has that `webcam-handler-cli`'s does not.** `cli_core::Command::record_request` refuses a `ReturnBytes` sink (note **N110**), a relative path, an extension naming a container this build does not write and a duration past `limits::MAX_RECORDING_MS` while a command line is being parsed, so a hand-written client is the only thing that can produce them; the rules themselves live on `schema::video::RecordRequest`, beside the variants they constrain, because `webcam-handler-daemon` links no `cli-core` (debt D-1, note **N46**). What makes each refusal *early* rather than merely correct is `FakeBackend::opens()` still being zero afterwards — a request this build was never going to honour must not cost anybody a descriptor — and none of the four leaves a file where none was. The second test is the seam's own: `engine::record::OnDisk` truncates because `File::create` does, and this daemon opens the destination **before** the camera without `O_TRUNC` (note **N51**: the length must not move until nothing can still refuse), so the truncation has to happen inside `Files::create` at the one moment `engine::record` guarantees nothing can still say no. Without it a short take written over a long one leaves the previous recording's tail past the end of the new file

**the preview is fed the recording's own frames** — the notes' Expected usage item 10, which said P6 owed an answer to a recording and a preview colliding on one camera and named the two honest options. The owner ruled on 2026-08-14 for the expensive one (note **N117**), and these three are it over a real socket: a tab that was already watching keeps painting on the request it already had while a take runs, a tab that arrives mid-take joins it, and a take that ends gives the camera back. Each of the three counts `streams_started` on the fake, which enforces one streamer per node exactly as V4L2 does — so a build that let the preview keep its own stream, or let `attach` start a second, answers a different number rather than failing on a picture somebody looked at

**the three edges of that ruling where a half-built version reads as working.** A camera that vanishes mid-take is collected as the device's own refusal *and* ends the readers' streams, because a take that failed must not reach either audience as the other's answer (AGENTS rule 7). A take D7 records raw feeds the fan-out nothing — those bytes are a broken image in an `` labelled `image/jpeg` — so they are dropped and **counted**, which is the only observable a frozen preview has (rubric rule 3). And a `wch_photo` during a take is `Busy` rather than a suspend, because `engine::preview::while_suspended` cannot tell a recording's stream from a preview's and stopping the wrong one puts a gap in the one measurement a recording exists to carry (note **N118**)

**`webcam-handler-cli record` end to end over both containers**, through the shipped binary and off committed profiles. What a subprocess suite adds over `crates/engine`'s own is the half nothing else covers: that the binary turns a command line into the request the engine gets, resolves a relative `-o` against the caller's directory the way D10 says, and puts the bytes where it said it did. The AVI arm re-parses the file with `imaging::avi::read::read_stream` and compares the frame count against the report's — either side alone is satisfiable by a build that lost the other — and asserts the `idx1` is there, which is what makes it the strict reader's file rather than a recoverable prefix. The Y4M arm runs over `corpus/profiles/chicony-ir.json`, a captured profile of a real **GREY-only** device, so all three of its claims are answers about hardware: `.y4m` records, a path with **no** extension is answered from the negotiated stream (the arm AGENTS' handless consumer depends on, since an agent that has not enumerated a camera cannot know which to type), and `.avi` is refused `FormatUnsupported` naming MJPG and JPEG — readable as FourCCs since note **N109**, which is what that ruling was for. The two renderings are compared on the three facts a person acts on, because `cli_core::render`'s rule is that a fact one mode shows and the other omits is a bug in the renderer

**one T4 verb over three wire methods, and the poll loop between them** — D10's "progress by polling `record_status`; no recording subscription in v1" as a thing that can go red. AGENTS is why the verb may not be three: *"a verb needing a call sequence … is a defect for the consumer that matters most"*, so `webcam-handler-client` owns the state machine exactly as it owns `calibrate_sweep`'s. The integration half runs the shipped client from a **directory of its own** and asks for `take.avi`: D10 resolves a relative `-o` on the caller's side before the request is sent, so the file has to appear there and not beside the daemon — a build that sent the relative path would either write it in the daemon's cwd or be refused `IllegalTransition`, and neither is a passing run. It then reads the file back and compares its length against the report's `bytes_written`, because that is what says the container was **closed** and therefore that the loop really waited. The three unit tests are about the only thing a loop can get wrong — when it stops: three answers cost three asks, a take already over costs one and no wait at all, a daemon that never says the take is over is given up on at `record_polls()` rather than waited for, and a refused poll ends the loop rather than turning one honest failure into hundreds. Every one of them drives the loop at `Duration::ZERO`, so no test here waits on a clock to find out whether the code works

**`record` is one verb on both roots**, which is the claim P6c exists to make and the reason the wire and the command surface had to land together: `cli-parity.sh` scrapes its population from `webcam-handler-cli --help`, so a `record` verb that existed before the wire did would put a leaf in no bucket and turn this gate red. Its row is `device` for `photo`'s reason — both roots replay the profile into a device state of their own, so a comparison would drive two devices and read back two answers about two of them — and for one of its own: a `RecordReport` carries `wall_clock_ms` and a summary measured on the driver's own frame timestamps, so two runs of one take differ by construction in the numbers that are the point of the verb, where the `stamped` bucket exists for a document that differs in exactly one field. What the exemption still buys is that bucket's own check, and for this verb it is worth more than for any other: `webcam-handler-client` has to **answer** it over the wire, which means all three of `record_start`, `record_status` and `record_stop` really ran against a running daemon

**`webcam-handler-cli record --json` validates against the committed bundle**, which is the half of the `--json` contract a type cannot state: the document is `RecordReport` verbatim — no envelope, no timestamp, no tool version — and `schemas/webcam-handler-schema.json` is what an agent validates it against. The three P6c roots (`RecordRequest`, `RecordReport`, `RecordStatus`) are registered by explicit `register::<T>` calls in `xtask`, so a verb whose answer type is not in the bundle fails here rather than at a consumer; `RecordingSummary`, `TakeStatus`, `VideoFormat`, `RecordingEnd`, `CapReached` and `IntervalSource` arrive as `$defs` by reachability, because a root is a document a `--json` verb emits or accepts and none of those is one on its own

**the committed artifacts describe the surface P6c closed.** A doc comment in `webcam-handler-api` or `webcam-handler-schema` is an input to a committed artifact rather than prose, and P6c writes a great deal of both: three method declarations, two new DTOs and a field on a third. The OpenRPC document grew by three `methods` entries and the JSON Schema bundle by three roots, and this predicate re-runs the emitter and diffs it — so the artifacts cannot describe a surface the daemon does not serve, in either direction

D10's account of the wire surface reconciled against the wire surface itself, which is the one compatibility contract in this project a consumer reads out of a document rather than out of the code (design §2.10 names D10 the wire surface's home). The fact is the `wire_surface!` invocation: the namespace literal jsonrpsee is handed and the `#[method]`/`#[subscription]` names it emits `METHODS` from. Three claims. **The namespace agrees** — G6 found the design naming `webcam-handler-cli`, which N90's rename sweep gave it while the macro kept `wch`, so a client author reading D10 sends `webcam-handler-cli_list` and is answered method not found; note N91, written in the same session, is the catalogue saying that this name is a wire break and must not be renamed in passing, and the warning and the breach landed together. **The method list is a derived population in both directions** — every name the macro declares must appear in D10 and every method-shaped name D10 states must be one the macro declares, which is what the abbreviation `calibrate_*` defeated: `calibrate_restore` was declared at P4a as the P3 review's one surface change and named nowhere in the design for two phases. **The committed OpenRPC document publishes that prefix and no other**, the half `schema-artifacts-current.sh` cannot say because both would move together under a rename. Two more sentences in the Rust carried the wrong name — one nine lines below the literal it contradicted — so the namespace claim is walked over every Rust source as well as the design; `docs/implementation-notes.md` and `docs/historical/` are out of reach rather than excluded, being records of a day. Sixteen arms, fourteen of them red on an inverse, the shipped tree and a wrapped design sentence green

**D7's CFR carve-out arriving at the second container**, which is what note **N106**'s amendment bought and the one thing in P6d that changed committed bytes rather than only inspecting them. N106 marked a zero-padded Y4M `F` denominator `declared` in this repository's sense — the format description permits decimal digits and says nothing about leading zeros, and nobody had driven a parser with one — and named the measurement that would retire it: *"the ffprobe/mpv oracle rung docs/7 P6d is about to build"*. That measurement is `E17`: `ffprobe` 8.0.1 reads `F1000000:0000050000` as `20/1` and `mpv` 0.41.0 as 20 fps, neither differing from the unpadded spelling. So the denominator is padded to ten digits (`u32::MAX` is ten, which is what makes it *fixed*-width rather than usually-wide-enough), `Y4mWriter::finish` patches the digits in place, and a Y4M take reports `IntervalSource::Measured`. Five claims and each is a separate way the rewrite could be half done: the header carries the mean and the summary agrees and the file's length did not move; the field's width does not depend on the interval and the patch is aimed at the denominator's own digits rather than one byte either side of them; a sink written into the middle of a file patches **its own** header and not somebody else's bytes (`origin`, which nothing else in that suite exercises); the walk over `VideoFormat::ALL` is now **one branch** where it was a two-armed `match`, so a third container has to answer the question rather than inherit an answer; and a take of one frame still says `Negotiated` in both, which is what stops the branch above being satisfiable by a container that answers `Measured` unconditionally. The decision itself moved to `imaging::video::declared_interval` — one home for a law two callers obey, which the asymmetry had been paying for

**the container-oracle harness can tell a good file from a damaged one**, which is the claim every other row in this phase rests on the moment it is quoted. `testkit::oracle` runs `ffprobe` and `mpv` over a file this workspace wrote, and what makes that worth having is stated in its own header: `imaging::avi::read` and `imaging::y4m`'s parser are independent of the muxers and are **not** independent of the people who wrote them, so a misreading shared by a writer and its reader is invisible to both. Three measurements shape the harness and each has an arm here. **`ffprobe`'s exit code is not a validity oracle** — every damaged file tried exits 0, and 1 means only that libavformat could not open the input — so the claims are judged on the JSON and `a_file_libavformat_cannot_open_at_all_is_a_failure_and_not_a_decline` holds the one thing the exit code does mean. **`nb_frames` is a header claim** (`avih.dwTotalFrames`, reported verbatim over a file holding nothing), so `a_file_with_no_frames_in_it_fails_however_many_its_header_claims` drives a zero-frame take against a four-frame expectation and watches both `ffprobe`'s count and `mpv`'s refusal to play it go red. And **a truncated JPEG still decodes**, so a file cut inside its last frame keeps every count it had: `a_frame_cut_in_half_fails_even_though_every_count_still_agrees` catches it on `pkt_size` alone and then asserts that the same file with the payload lengths withheld is **green**, which is what makes the sentence a measurement rather than a hope. `every_host_the_fault_menu_names_declines_by_name_rather_than_passing` walks `HostFault::ALL` against a host it invents, because both oracles are installed on the machine this landed on and a decline nobody has watched fire is a decline nobody can trust — and it asserts the decline *lines* without printing them, since a fabricated absence in the run log is read by the runner as this host lacking a tool it has

**the oracle rung runs or reports a named, counted skip — never silence** (docs/9's "Oracle rung accounting" row, AGENTS rule 3, which names this rung by name). A `command` row rather than a filterset for `just gate-g5`'s R1-web reason in its own words: what the gate close records is not a test count but *which of two things happened*. Design §3.1 names R0, R1, R1-web, R2 and R3 and no oracle letter, and inventing one would amend a settled section — so this rung has a name and no letter, its fake-generated half hangs off the every-push rungs (`crates/engine/tests/oracles.rs`, not `#[ignore]`d, with `success-output = "final"` in `.config/nextest.toml` so a decline is never printed into a void) and its real-camera half is part of R3. The runner ends on RAN, on SKIPPED with every decline reprinted and its remedy named, or on one of two FAILs — and the second of those is the reason the shape is copied from `rung-web.sh` rather than invented: a run that printed **neither** a decline nor a run line is a failure, because a rung nobody can tell apart from one that was never invoked is the defect class the whole ladder exists for
